title: Privacy timeline anchors

anchors.label: Private / privacy as solitary, secluded state
anchors.description: Earliest dictionary traditions describe related 'private' usage as secluded or apart from public view. The noun privacy is later used to encode this meaning indirectly and with uneven standardization.
anchors.notes: Date estimate is intentionally cautious; early usage differs across historical sources.

anchors.label: Toward freedom from intrusion framing
anchors.description: Shift from descriptive 'private/secluded' meaning toward civic concern about unwanted observation and interference appears in 19th-century legal/philosophical treatments.
anchors.source: Historical legal and language scholarship references
anchors.notes: Used as an approximate turning window for first-pass planning.

anchors.label: Warren and Brandeis publish 'The Right to Privacy'
anchors.description: Defines privacy as 'the right to be let alone', introducing legal discourse around intrusion in American public law.
anchors.source: Warren & Brandeis, The Right to Privacy, 1890
anchors.notes: Anchorable publication year for modern legal privacy discourse.

anchors.label: Mid-century privacy/legal commentary consolidates
anchors.description: Privacy language continues in legal journalism and constitutional discussion around informational and personal autonomy boundaries.
anchors.notes: Broad period marker; used as context, not single-source claim.

anchors.label: US Privacy Act and early information-privacy law
anchors.description: Federal privacy framework begins to regulate U.S. federal agency handling of personal records.
anchors.notes: Strong legal source, limited to U.S. federal agencies and records handling.

anchors.label: Privacy in information systems and policy recommendations
anchors.description: The OECD begins to frame data protection principles for automated systems and personal data handling.
anchors.notes: The exact principle text is broad and often implemented via derivative documents.

anchors.label: United Kingdom enacts Data Protection Act
anchors.description: A major legal move toward codified personal data rights and processing limitations.
anchors.notes: Sourceable in legal records; later replaced/amended by the 2018 UK regime.

anchors.label: Digital identity and cross-border data risk become explicit policy concerns
anchors.description: The early web era pushes 'online privacy' into mainstream regulatory and consumer discussion.
anchors.source: Public policy literature on internet governance and data security
anchors.notes: Used as a context marker for internet-facing privacy concerns.

anchors.label: Privacy settings and privacy-policy language become user-facing platform defaults
anchors.description: Web services begin offering explicit consent and account-level controls tied to privacy claims.
anchors.source: Platform policy history (policy terms and settings conventions)
anchors.notes: Conservative marker for the shift to product-level governance language.

anchors.label: Post-surveillance leak era re-centers security versus privacy
anchors.description: Public attention moves sharply toward state monitoring, corporate surveillance, and security trade-offs.
anchors.notes: Year used as a broad shift marker for narrative planning.

anchors.label: GDPR-era platform-era privacy obligations
anchors.description: Globalization of data rights and platform accountability through modern privacy frameworks.
anchors.source: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) and follow-on summaries

anchors.label: AI and algorithmic inference expand data-privacy risk surface
anchors.description: AI-era privacy claims connect model training, inference, and automated decision risks with individual autonomy.
anchors.source: OECD/academic AI governance and data rights work
anchors.notes: Low confidence for year-level precision; use as a modern directional anchor only.

notes: Anchors are intended for narrative planning and annotation, not final claims.
Low-confidence anchors should be reviewed against primary sources before chart publication.
Source status in the scrape checks reachability only (not full content validation).
source_notes: Mixed source quality and scope (dictionary entries, legal text, policy summaries, and regulations).
Early-century lexical anchors are especially uncertain and intentionally marked low-confidence.
AI-era anchors are modern and directionally useful even where year precision varies.
